abstract: Azar, Gine and Sanz-Espin study how generative AI has affected wages and worker mobility in US knowledge-intensive service industries (NAICS 51-56), using the public release of ChatGPT on 30 November 2022 as a common shock. Their central result is that the early labor market response to GenAI shows up in the price of labor and in worker mobility rather than in headcount. Moving from the 10th to the 90th percentile of occupational GenAI exposure is associated with a 4.9% decline in real median hourly wages in OEWS 2025 data, an 8.71% decline in Revelio posted wages, and a 10.76% decline in Revelio starting wages by 2026 - with no statistically detectable change in employment. The wage decline is steeply graded by position in the firm hierarchy: by 2026 the same exposure contrast implies declines of roughly 7.5% for junior positions, 3.2% for mid-level, and a statistically insignificant 1.8% for senior. Crucially, this is a rank effect rather than an age effect - wage declines appear among junior workers in every age band, including those over 40, and the largest point estimate is among junior workers older than 40. Alongside the wage decline, separations fall 3.0 percentage points (18.6% of the pre-ChatGPT mean), driven almost entirely by job-to-job transitions (down 2.8pp, or 28.8%), while separations into persistent non-employment are unchanged. Separations also become markedly less responsive to posted wages at high exposure, which under an inverse-elasticity benchmark implies wage markdowns rising 38.2% to 75.1% across exposure quintiles. The authors' framing is that outside opportunities deteriorate before existing jobs disappear.
keyFindings: 4.9% decline in real median hourly wages moving from the 10th to the 90th percentile of GenAI exposure (OEWS, 2025); the 2024 estimate is 6.7% and the pooled post-ChatGPT average is 4.6%.

8.71% decline in posted wages and 10.76% decline in starting wages over the same P10-to-P90 exposure contrast (Revelio, by 2026); the 2026 figure carries a caveat because the Revelio vintage ends in June 2026.

No statistically detectable employment effect. OEWS post-ChatGPT employment coefficients are insignificant and show no sustained downward path, and there is no increase in separations to persistent non-employment.
Seniority gradient by 2026: 7.5% wage decline for junior positions, 3.2% for mid-level, 1.8% (insignificant) for senior. Pooled estimates are 4.2%, 2.5%, and 1.8%.

The junior effect is a rank effect, not a young-worker effect: significant wage declines appear among junior workers aged 22-30, 31-40, and 41-70, with the largest point estimate among junior workers older than 40.

Separation rate falls 3.0 percentage points (18.6% of the pre-ChatGPT mean); job-to-job transitions fall 2.8pp (28.8%), accounting for about 92% of the total, while persistent-non-employment separations are statistically unchanged.

Workers reporting GenAI-related skills earn a conditional starting-wage premium of roughly 8-9%, yet the coefficient on the cell-level GenAI worker share is negative (-0.151 alone, -0.122 with exposure included) - an individual premium coexisting with lower wages where those skills are widespread.

Separation elasticities attenuate most at high exposure. Under the Manning inverse-elasticity benchmark, implied relative wage markdowns rise 38.2% at the lowest exposure quintile to 75.1% at the highest.
Effects concentrate in Information (-0.195), Finance and Insurance (-0.127), and Professional Services (-0.092), and increase with firm size (-0.066 under 50 employees; -0.146 above 250).
methodology: Continuous-treatment difference-in-differences using the 30 November 2022 ChatGPT release as a common shock, with 2022 as the omitted reference year. Two datasets, both restricted to knowledge-intensive service industries (NAICS 51-56). (1) OEWS: balanced 2018-2025 panel of 24,736 six-digit SOC occupation by four-digit NAICS industry-year observations, covering 3,092 cells, 431 occupations, and 37 industries; outcome is CPI-deflated log median hourly wage; occupation-by-industry and industry-by-year fixed effects; stabilized nonparametric inverse-probability weights times 2022 employment; standard errors clustered by three-digit NAICS. (2) Revelio: balanced 2018-2026 panel of 15,218,901 firm-by-SOC6-by-MSA cell-year observations across 1,690,989 cells, drawn from a US base of over 490 million observations and 148 million workers; outcomes are real log starting wages of new positions, posted wages, and worker-flow rates; firm-by-occupation-by-MSA, firm-by-year, and MSA-by-year fixed effects; standard errors two-way clustered by firm and occupation. Treatment is the Eloundou et al. (2024) occupation-level GenAI exposure index, held fixed and, in Revelio, constructed from each cell's detailed O*NET composition as of 30 November 2022. Work-from-home exposure (Hansen et al. 2023) is interacted with year indicators throughout to address the remote-work confound. Separation elasticities use an AKM-IV design instrumenting posted wages with a cross-fitted firm wage component following Bassier et al. (2022), in both linear and restricted-cubic-spline specifications.
qualifiers: Tier 2: SSRN working paper, not peer-reviewed, previously circulated as 'AI Is Already Eroding Wages: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from Occupational Exposure'. The design identifies differential changes across the exposure distribution, not aggregate effects - the authors are explicit that 'our coefficients therefore capture differential changes across the exposure distribution, not the aggregate effect of ChatGPT on the labor market,' and that occupations with low direct exposure may still be affected through spillovers or general equilibrium. Exposure measures susceptibility to the technology, not actual adoption; the index tells us nothing about which firms deployed GenAI or how intensively. Scope is limited to knowledge-intensive service industries, so results should not be read as economy-wide. Magnitudes are sensitive to weighting: OEWS estimates range from -0.021 (no inverse-probability weights) to -0.116 (parametric weights) against a -0.078 baseline, though the sign is stable across every robustness specification. The 2026 Revelio estimates rest on a vintage ending June 2026 and the authors flag them for caution. Revelio starting wages are partly imputed, combining postings, self-reported salary sites, H-1B filings, and CPS; correlation with OEWS wages is 0.81. The GenAI-skills exercises are explicitly descriptive, not causal returns to skill acquisition, since reported skills may respond to wages and worker composition. The markdown calculations are illustrative calibrations under the inverse-elasticity rule, not estimates of firms' structural markdowns or workers' marginal products, and may fail under bargaining, non-wage amenities, or internal pay norms. A causal reading still requires that no remaining post-2022 shock correlates with predetermined exposure after conditioning. The authors close by noting the estimates cover only the first few years and 'the longer-run response may therefore look different.'
